putnam-1998-a1.title: Cross-section through a diagonal
putnam-1998-a1.body:
Let $s$ be the side of the cube. By symmetry the cube's vertical axis is the cone's axis, and its four top vertices lie on the cone's surface.

Cut by the vertical plane through the axis and two opposite vertical edges of the cube. It meets the cone in an isosceles triangle with base $2$ and height $3$, and the cube in a rectangle of width $s\sqrt2$ (the diagonal of a face) and height $s$, standing on the base with its top corners on the slanted sides.

At height $h$ the cone's radius is $1 - \frac h3$. The top corners are at height $s$ and distance $\frac{s\sqrt2}{2}$ from the axis, so
$$\frac{s\sqrt2}{2} = 1-\frac s3 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad s\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}+\frac13\right) = 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad s = \frac{6}{3\sqrt2+2} = \frac{6(3\sqrt2-2)}{18-4} = \frac{9\sqrt2-6}{7}.$$

**Answer: $s = \dfrac{9\sqrt2-6}{7}\approx 0.961$**

putnam-1998-a2.title: Integrate in the angle
putnam-1998-a2.body:
Let $s$ consist of the points $(\cos t,\sin t)$ for $\alpha\le t\le\beta$, where $0\le\alpha<\beta\le\frac\pi2$; its length is $\beta-\alpha$.

Over $x\in[\cos\beta,\cos\alpha]$ the arc is the graph $y = \sqrt{1-x^2}$, so with $x = \cos t$, $dx = -\sin t\,dt$:
$$A = \int_{\cos\beta}^{\cos\alpha}\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\sin^2 t\,dt.$$
Likewise over $y\in[\sin\alpha,\sin\beta]$ the arc is the graph $x = \sqrt{1-y^2}$, and with $y = \sin t$:
$$B = \int_{\sin\alpha}^{\sin\beta}\sqrt{1-y^2}\,dy = \int_\alpha^\beta \cos^2 t\,dt.$$
Adding, $A + B = \int_\alpha^\beta (\sin^2t+\cos^2t)\,dt = \beta - \alpha$, the arc length of $s$. ∎

putnam-1998-a2.title: Sectors and triangles
putnam-1998-a2.body:
Let $O$ be the origin and let the arc run from $E = (\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)$ to $D = (\cos\beta,\sin\beta)$ with $0 \le \alpha < \beta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$. Let $F, G$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $D, E$ to the $x$-axis, and $H, I$ the feet of the perpendiculars from $D, E$ to the $y$-axis. Let $C$ be the area of the sector $ODE$; it equals $\frac{\beta-\alpha}{2}$.

Triangle $OGE$ together with sector $ODE$ is the region bounded by $O\to G\to E\to(\text{arc})\to D\to O$; removing the triangle $ODF$ leaves exactly the region $FGE(\text{arc})D$ under the arc. So
$$A = C + [OEG] - [ODF] = C + \tfrac12\cos\alpha\sin\alpha - \tfrac12\cos\beta\sin\beta.$$
Symmetrically, $B = C + [ODH] - [OEI] = C + \tfrac12\cos\beta\sin\beta - \tfrac12\cos\alpha\sin\alpha$.

Adding, $A + B = 2C = \beta-\alpha$, which depends only on the length of the arc. ∎

putnam-1998-a3.title: Sign normalization and convexity
putnam-1998-a3.body:
Suppose, for contradiction, that $f f' f'' f''' < 0$ everywhere. Then none of $f,f',f'',f'''$ vanishes anywhere, and since they are continuous, each has a constant sign on $\mathbb R$ (intermediate value theorem).

**Normalization.** Replacing $f$ by $-f$ changes the sign of all four functions, so the product is unchanged; replacing $f(x)$ by $f(-x)$ multiplies $f,f',f'',f'''$ by $1,-1,1,-1$, again leaving the product unchanged, and it does not change the sign of $f''$. So we may assume first $f''>0$ and then $f'''>0$.

**$f' > 0$.** Since $f''' > 0$, the derivative $f''$ of $g = f'$ is increasing, so $g$ is convex and lies above its tangent lines: for all $x,t$, $f'(x+t)\ge f'(x) + t f''(x)$. Fix $x$; as $f''(x)>0$, the right side is positive for large $t$, so $f'$ takes a positive value. As $f'$ has constant sign, $f'>0$ everywhere.

**$f > 0$.** Since $f''>0$, $f$ is convex: $f(x+t)\ge f(x) + t f'(x)$, and $f'(x) > 0$ gives positive values for large $t$. Hence $f > 0$ everywhere.

Now $f f' f'' f''' > 0$, contradicting the assumption. So some $a$ has $f(a)f'(a)f''(a)f'''(a)\ge0$. ∎

putnam-1998-a4.title: Recurrence modulo 11
putnam-1998-a4.body:
**Lengths.** Let $L_n$ be the number of digits of $A_n$. For $n\ge2$, $A_n$ starts with the digit $1$ (it starts with $A_{n-1}$, and ultimately with $A_2 = 1$), so concatenation gives $A_n = A_{n-1}\cdot 10^{L_{n-2}} + A_{n-2}$ and $L_n = L_{n-1}+L_{n-2}$. With $L_1 = L_2 = 1$, $L_n = F_n$ is the Fibonacci number.

**Mod 11.** Since $10\equiv -1\pmod{11}$,
$$A_n \equiv (-1)^{F_{n-2}}A_{n-1} + A_{n-2}\pmod{11}\qquad(n\ge3).$$
The Fibonacci numbers mod 2 are $1,1,0,1,1,0,\dots$: $F_j$ is even iff $3\mid j$. So the sign depends only on $n \bmod 3$: it is $+$ when $n\equiv 2\pmod 3$ and $-$ otherwise.

**Compute.** Starting from $A_1 = 0$, $A_2 = 1$:
$$A_3\equiv -1,\quad A_4 \equiv 1+1 = 2,\quad A_5\equiv 2 + (-1) = 1,\quad A_6 \equiv -1 + 2 = 1,\quad A_7 \equiv -1+1 = 0,\quad A_8\equiv 0+1 = 1.$$
(Check: $A_3 = 10\equiv -1$, $A_4 = 101 \equiv 2$, $A_5 = 10110 = 11\cdot 919 + 1$.)

**Periodicity.** $(A_7,A_8)\equiv(A_1,A_2)$, and the sign in the recurrence has period $3$, which divides $6$. By induction $A_{n+6}\equiv A_n \pmod{11}$ for all $n\ge1$. Among $A_1,\dots,A_6 \equiv 0,1,-1,2,1,1$ only $A_1$ is $\equiv 0$.

**Answer:** $11\mid A_n$ if and only if $n\equiv 1\pmod 6$. ∎

putnam-1998-a5.title: Greedy choice of the largest discs
putnam-1998-a5.body:
**Construction.** Let $D_1$ be a disc of largest radius in $\mathcal F$. Having chosen $D_1,\dots,D_i$, let $D_{i+1}$ be a disc of largest radius among the discs of $\mathcal F$ disjoint from $D_1\cup\dots\cup D_i$; stop when there is none. Since $\mathcal F$ is finite this stops, with pairwise disjoint discs $D_1,\dots,D_n$. (If $\mathcal F$ is empty then $E$ is empty and there is nothing to prove.)

**Key claim.** Every $D\in\mathcal F$ is contained in some $3D_i$.

If $D$ is one of the $D_i$, this is clear. Otherwise $D$ meets some chosen disc (or the algorithm would not have stopped); let $D_i$ be the first chosen disc meeting $D$. When $D_i$ was chosen, $D$ was disjoint from $D_1,\dots,D_{i-1}$, so $D$ was a candidate; hence $r_i\ge r$, where $r_i$ and $r$ are the radii of $D_i$ and $D$.

Let $P_i$, $P$ be the centers. Two open discs intersect only if $|PP_i| < r + r_i$. For any point $X\in D$,
$$|XP_i| \le |XP| + |PP_i| < r + (r + r_i) \le 3r_i,$$
so $X\in 3D_i$. This proves the claim.

**Conclusion.** $E\subseteq\bigcup_{D\in\mathcal F} D \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^n 3D_i$. ∎

putnam-1998-a6.title: Squeeze between integers
putnam-1998-a6.body:
Let $a = |AB|$, $c = |BC|$, $S = [ABC]$.

**Integrality.** $a^2$ and $c^2$ are integers (Pythagoras with integer coordinates), and $2S$ is an integer (with $B$ at the origin and $A=(p,q)$, $C = (u,w)$, $2S = |pw - qu|$). So $a^2 + c^2 + 4S$ and $8S$ are integers.

**Inequalities.** $2S = ac\sin\angle B\le ac$, and $a^2+c^2\ge 2ac$. Hence
$$8S = 4S + 4S \le a^2 + c^2 + 4S \le a^2+c^2+2ac = (a+c)^2 < 8S+1.$$
The integer $a^2+c^2+4S$ lies in $[8S, 8S+1)$ where $8S$ is an integer, so $a^2+c^2+4S = 8S$, i.e. $a^2+c^2 = 4S$.

**Equality case.** Now $4S = a^2+c^2\ge 2ac\ge 4S$, so both inequalities are equalities: $a = c$ and $ac = 2S = ac\sin\angle B$. As $a,c>0$ (distinct points), $\sin\angle B = 1$, so $\angle B = 90^\circ$.

Thus $BA$ and $BC$ are perpendicular segments of equal length, and $A$, $B$, $C$ are three vertices of the square $ABCD$ with $D = A + C - B$. ∎

putnam-1998-b1.title: Difference of squares
putnam-1998-b1.body:
Let $u = (x+1/x)^3$ and $v = x^3+1/x^3$. Since $v^2 = x^6 + 2 + 1/x^6$, the numerator is $u^2 - v^2$ and the denominator is $u+v>0$. So the expression equals
$$u - v = \left(x^3 + 3x + \frac3x + \frac1{x^3}\right) - \left(x^3+\frac1{x^3}\right) = 3\left(x+\frac1x\right).$$
By AM–GM, $x + \frac1x\ge2$ with equality at $x = 1$. So the minimum is $6$, attained at $x=1$.

**Answer: $6$**

putnam-1998-b1.title: Substitute $t = x + 1/x$
putnam-1998-b1.body:
Let $t = x+1/x\ge 2$. Then $x^3+1/x^3 = t^3 - 3t$ and $x^6+1/x^6 = (t^3-3t)^2 - 2$. The expression becomes
$$\frac{t^6 - (t^3-3t)^2 + 2 - 2}{t^3 + t^3 - 3t} = \frac{6t^4 - 9t^2}{2t^3-3t} = \frac{3t^2(2t^2-3)}{t(2t^2-3)} = 3t,$$
which is minimal for $t = 2$ (i.e. $x=1$): the minimum is $6$.

**Answer: $6$**

putnam-1998-b2.title: Two reflections
putnam-1998-b2.body:
Let $A = (a,b)$, let $B$ be the vertex on the $x$-axis and $C$ the vertex on the line $y = x$. Reflect $A$ in the $x$-axis to get $D = (a,-b)$ and in the line $y=x$ to get $E = (b,a)$. Then $AB = DB$ and $AC = EC$, so
$$AB + BC + CA = DB + BC + CE \ge DE = \sqrt{(a-b)^2 + (a+b)^2} = \sqrt{2a^2+2b^2}$$
by the triangle inequality along the path $D\to B\to C\to E$.

**The bound is attained.** Parametrize segment $DE$ as $D + t(E-D) = \big(a + t(b-a),\ -b + t(a+b)\big)$, $0\le t\le 1$. It meets the $x$-axis at $t_B = \frac{b}{a+b}$ and the line $y=x$ at $t_C = \frac{a+b}{2a}$. Since $0<b<a$: $0 < t_B < t_C < 1$ (the middle inequality is $2ab < (a+b)^2$, the last is $b<a$). Taking $B$, $C$ at these points, $D, B, C, E$ lie in this order on the segment, so $DB + BC + CE = DE$. 

Hence the minimum perimeter is $\sqrt{2a^2+2b^2} = \sqrt2\,\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$. ∎

putnam-1998-b3.title: Subtract five half-caps
putnam-1998-b3.body:
**Archimedes' cap formula.** The part of the unit sphere with $x\ge h$ ($-1\le h\le1$) has area $2\pi(1-h)$. Indeed it is the surface of revolution of $y = \sqrt{1-x^2}$, $h\le x\le 1$, about the $x$-axis, with area
$$\int_h^1 2\pi y\sqrt{1+y'^2}\,dx = \int_h^1 2\pi\sqrt{1-x^2}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,dx = 2\pi(1-h).$$

**Decomposition.** The unit disc is the pentagon together with five congruent circular segments cut off by its sides (overlapping only in boundaries, which have zero area). Each side lies at distance $d = \cos\frac\pi5$ from the center (the apothem of a regular pentagon with circumradius $1$). After a rotation about the $z$-axis, a segment is $\{x\ge d\}$ in the disc, and the part of $H$ above it is $\{x\ge d,\ z\ge0\}$ on the sphere — by the symmetry $z\mapsto -z$, exactly half of a cap of area $2\pi(1-d)$.

**Area.** The hemisphere has area $2\pi$, so the requested area is
$$2\pi - 5\cdot\frac{2\pi(1-\cos\frac\pi5)}{2} = 5\pi\cos\frac\pi5 - 3\pi.$$
This has the requested form, e.g. with $A = -3\pi$, $\alpha = \frac\pi2$, $B = 5\pi$, $\beta = \frac\pi5$. Numerically, since $\cos\frac\pi5 = \frac{1+\sqrt5}{4}$, it equals $\frac{(5\sqrt5-7)\pi}{4}\approx 3.283$.

**Answer: $5\pi\cos\frac{\pi}{5} - 3\pi$**

putnam-1998-b4.title: Parity cases and halving
putnam-1998-b4.body:
Write $f_{m,n}(i) = \lfloor i/m\rfloor + \lfloor i/n\rfloor$ and $S(m,n) = \sum_{i=0}^{mn-1}(-1)^{f_{m,n}(i)}$. Let $v_2$ denote the exponent of $2$. We show $S(m,n) = 0 \iff v_2(m)\ne v_2(n)$, by induction on $m+n$.

**Both odd** ($v_2(m) = v_2(n) = 0$). $S$ is a sum of $mn$ terms $\pm1$, an odd number, so $S\ne 0$.

**Opposite parity** ($v_2(m)\ne v_2(n)$). Write $i = qm + r$ with $0\le r<m$; then $mn-1-i = (n-1-q)m + (m-1-r)$ with $0\le m-1-r<m$, so $\lfloor i/m\rfloor + \lfloor (mn-1-i)/m\rfloor = n-1$. Similarly $\lfloor i/n\rfloor + \lfloor (mn-1-i)/n\rfloor = m-1$. Hence
$$f_{m,n}(i) + f_{m,n}(mn-1-i) = m+n-2,$$
which is odd. So the terms for $i$ and $mn-1-i$ cancel (and $i\ne mn-1-i$, as otherwise $2f(i)$ would be odd). Thus $S = 0$.

**Both even**, $m = 2k$, $n = 2l$. For $j = qk + r$ ($0\le r<k$) both $2j = 2qk+2r$ and $2j+1 \le 2qk + 2k - 1$ have $\lfloor\cdot/(2k)\rfloor = q = \lfloor j/k\rfloor$; similarly for $n$. So the terms $i = 2j$ and $i = 2j+1$ are equal to $(-1)^{f_{k,l}(j)}$, and
$$S(2k,2l) = 2\sum_{j=0}^{2kl-1}(-1)^{f_{k,l}(j)}.$$
For $0 \le j < kl$, $f_{k,l}(j+kl) = f_{k,l}(j) + l + k$, so the second half of this sum is $(-1)^{k+l}$ times the first half:
$$S(2k,2l) = 2\big(1+(-1)^{k+l}\big)S(k,l).$$
If $k+l$ is even, $S(2k,2l) = 4S(k,l)$. If $k+l$ is odd, then $S(2k,2l) = 0$ and also $S(k,l) = 0$ (opposite parity case). Either way $S(2k,2l) = 0\iff S(k,l) = 0 \iff v_2(k)\ne v_2(l)$ (induction) $\iff v_2(m)\ne v_2(n)$.

**Answer:** the sum vanishes if and only if the highest powers of $2$ dividing $m$ and $n$ are different. ∎

putnam-1998-b5.title: Expand the square root
putnam-1998-b5.body:
$N = \frac{10^{1998}-1}{9}$, so with $\varepsilon = 10^{-1998}$,
$$\sqrt N = \frac{\sqrt{10^{1998}-1}}{3} = \frac{10^{999}}{3}\sqrt{1-\varepsilon}.$$

**Bounds for the root.** For $0<\varepsilon<1$: $(1-\frac\varepsilon2)^2 = 1-\varepsilon+\frac{\varepsilon^2}{4} > 1-\varepsilon$, and with $\sigma = \frac\varepsilon2+\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}$, $(1-\sigma)^2 = 1 - \varepsilon - \varepsilon^2 + \sigma^2 < 1-\varepsilon$ (as $\sigma < \varepsilon$). Hence
$$\sqrt N = \frac{10^{999}}{3} - \frac{10^{-999}}{6} - \delta,\qquad 0 < \delta < \frac{10^{999}}{3}\cdot\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2} = \frac{10^{-2997}}{6}.$$

**Digits.** $\frac{10^{999}}{3} = \frac{10^{999}-1}{3} + \frac13$, where $\frac{10^{999}-1}{3} = 33\ldots3$ is an integer. So the fractional part of $\sqrt N$ is
$$\frac13 - \frac{10^{-999}}{6} - \delta = 0.\underbrace{33\ldots3}_{999} + 10^{-999}\Big(\frac13 - \frac16 - 10^{999}\delta\Big) = 0.\underbrace{33\ldots3}_{999} + 10^{-999}\Big(\frac16 - 10^{999}\delta\Big),$$
and $0.1 < \frac16 - 10^{999}\delta < \frac16 < 0.2$ because $10^{999}\delta < 10^{-1998}$. So the decimal expansion is $0.33\ldots3\,1\,6\ldots$ with $999$ threes followed by the digit $1$ in position $1000$.

**Answer: $1$**

putnam-1998-b6.title: Work modulo 4
putnam-1998-b6.body:
Let $p(n) = n^3 + an^2 + bn + c$. Suppose, for contradiction, that $p(n)$ is a perfect square for every positive integer $n$.

Compute
$$p(n+2) - p(n) = (6n^2+12n+8) + a(4n+4) + 2b \equiv 2n^2 + 2b \pmod 4.$$
Choose $n\in\{1,2\}$ with $n\not\equiv b\pmod 2$. Then $n^2 + b$ is odd, so $p(n+2)-p(n)\equiv 2\pmod 4$.

But squares are $\equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 4$, so the difference of two squares is $\equiv 0, 1$ or $3\pmod 4$, never $2$. Hence $p(n)$ and $p(n+2)$ cannot both be perfect squares, a contradiction. So for $n$ or $n+2$ the number $\sqrt{p(\cdot)}$ is not an integer (it is not even real if $p(\cdot) < 0$). ∎

putnam-1998-b6.title: Growth: squares are too sparse
putnam-1998-b6.body:
Suppose $p(n) = n^3+an^2+bn+c$ is a perfect square for all $n\ge1$. Take $n = 4k^2$ (an even perfect square), so $n^{3/2} = 8k^3$ and $n^{1/2} = 2k$ are integers, and let $M = n^{3/2} + \frac a2 n^{1/2} = 8k^3 + ak$, an integer. Then
$$(M\pm1)^2 = n^3 + an^2 + \tfrac{a^2}{4}n \pm 2\big(n^{3/2}+\tfrac a2 n^{1/2}\big)+1,$$
so $p(n) - (M-1)^2 = 2n^{3/2} + O(n)$ and $(M+1)^2 - p(n) = 2n^{3/2} + O(n)$, both positive for large $k$. So for large $k$, $(M-1)^2 < p(n) < (M+1)^2$, and as $p(n)$ is a square of a nonnegative integer it must equal $M^2$:
$$n^3 + an^2 + bn + c = n^3 + an^2 + \tfrac{a^2}{4}n \quad\text{for } n = 4k^2,\ k \text{ large}.$$
Infinitely many $n$ satisfy $\big(b - \frac{a^2}4\big)n + c = 0$, so $c = 0$ and $b = \frac{a^2}{4}$; then $a$ is even, $a = 2e$, and $p(n) = n(n+e)^2$. Pick $n\in\{2,3\}$ with $n+e\ne0$. If $n(n+e)^2 = m^2$ for an integer $m$, then $n = \big(m/(n+e)\big)^2$ would be the square of a rational number, hence of an integer — but $2$ and $3$ are not squares. Contradiction. ∎
